explanation: Regular-way settlement finalizes ownership and payment for standard U.S. equities one business day after the trade date. Five business days, two business days, and finality on the trade date are different timing rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Five business days was an older equity cycle; regular-way ownership and payment now finalize one business day after the trade date.
distractorExplanations.c: Finality on the trade date is not regular-way settlement for standard U.S. equities, which finalize on the next business day.
distractorExplanations.d: Two business days was the prior regular-way cycle; standard equity obligations now finalize one business day after the trade.

prompt: For a voluntary corporate action such as a tender offer, operations must:

options.text: Apply the default option to each holder on the effective date without notice
Notify customers and accept elections up to the payable date set by the issuer
Notify customers, collect elections by deadline, and submit instructions
Tender shares for each holder and let customers withdraw before the offer expires

explanation: Voluntary actions require timely client communication and accurate election processing. Instructions are submitted to the issuer's tender or exchange agent.

distractorExplanations.a: Defaults apply only when a holder does not respond after notice; a voluntary offer requires notifying holders and collecting elections first.
distractorExplanations.b: Elections must arrive before the firm's internal deadline ahead of offer expiration; the payable date comes after the offer closes.
distractorExplanations.d: The firm cannot tender without instructions; in a voluntary offer customers opt in rather than being tendered and opting out.

prompt: Employer restricted stock deposited to a brokerage account typically requires:

options.text: Legend removal by the firm's own operations team once the shares are deposited
Holding the shares for one year before any sale, as Rule 144 requires
Filing Form 144 for any sale, even when shares are freely tradable
Restriction legend tracking, release schedules, and compliance with Rule 144

explanation: Ops tracks control restrictions and release dates before unrestricted trading. Rule 144 compliance applies where the shares are restricted or held by an affiliate.

distractorExplanations.a: The issuer's transfer agent removes a legend, typically after an issuer or counsel opinion; the firm's ops team cannot remove it.
distractorExplanations.b: For an SEC-reporting issuer the Rule 144 holding period is six months; one year applies to non-reporting issuers, so a blanket hold is wrong.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 144 is needed for affiliate or restricted sales above 5,000 shares or $50,000 in three months, not for any freely tradable sale.

prompt: When a customer requests an outbound wire from a brokerage account, operations should first:

options.text: Verify authorization, confirm payee details, and apply fraud controls per firm policy
Confirm the request with an email reply to the address on file, then release the wire
Verify authorization when the wire pays a third party, but not when it pays the customer's own bank
Release the wire now and complete identity verification after the wire has settled

explanation: Wire fraud controls include callback to number on file and hold periods for new payees.

distractorExplanations.b: Email confirmation can be intercepted by a fraudster who controls the mailbox; a callback to a phone number on file is the standard.
distractorExplanations.c: First-party wires to a newly linked bank are a top takeover path; authorization and payee checks apply to first-party wires too.
distractorExplanations.d: Verification after release is too late; wired funds are hard to recall, so controls must run before release.

prompt: Processing a mandatory cash merger typically requires operations to:

options.text: Collect customer elections before crediting cash on payment date
Remove target shares and credit cash proceeds on payment date
Credit cash proceeds on the record date and remove shares at payment
Remove target shares and credit acquirer stock at the exchange ratio

explanation: Mandatory mergers exchange shares for cash and/or acquirer stock per terms on effective date. Corporate action entries are posted to each account on the payment date.

distractorExplanations.a: Elections are for voluntary or cash/stock election deals; a mandatory cash merger is processed for every holder without instructions.
distractorExplanations.c: In a cash merger, shares are removed and cash credited together on payment date; the record date does not trigger the cash credit.
distractorExplanations.d: Crediting acquirer stock describes a stock-for-stock merger; a cash merger pays a fixed cash amount per share.

prompt: A fail to deliver in equities settlement may result from:

options.text: A customer selling long shares the firm already holds fully paid in street name
Customer buying shares on margin instead of paying in full by T+1
Short seller lacking locate/borrow or deliverer missing shares at settlement
Short seller obtaining a locate and borrowing shares before settlement

explanation: A fail to deliver happens when the selling side cannot produce the shares on settlement. That is a short sale with no locate or borrow, or a long sale the firm cannot find. A long sale of shares already in street name, a margin purchase, and a short that was located and borrowed do not create that fail.

distractorExplanations.a: Long sales from fully paid street-name positions are deliverable from the firm's DTC account and do not cause fails.
distractorExplanations.b: Margin purchases are financed by the firm and settle normally; how a buyer pays does not create a fail to deliver.
distractorExplanations.d: A locate plus a borrow before settlement lets the seller deliver; that prevents rather than causes a fail.

prompt: Customer check deposits to a brokerage account require operations to:

options.text: Make check funds available for trading and withdrawal the next business day
Apply a fixed 10-business-day hold set by FINRA to every check deposit
Hold funds for trading but permit wires out of the account immediately
Apply hold periods per firm policy and applicable funds-availability rules

explanation: Broker-dealers apply hold schedules and fraud controls on check deposits; bank-like Reg CC schedules may inform policy but the firm’s procedures govern release for trading. Holds apply before funds are released for trading.

distractorExplanations.a: Next-day availability for withdrawals invites returned-check fraud; firms hold funds per policy until the check is collected.
distractorExplanations.b: FINRA sets no uniform check-hold period; hold schedules come from firm policy informed by funds-availability rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiring out uncollected funds is the highest-risk release; restricting trading but not withdrawals inverts the control.

prompt: A short American-style equity option can be assigned:

options.text: On any business day the long holder exercises, including before expiration
Only on expiration day, since early exercise applies to European options
On the day OCC receives exercise notice, with assignment deferred to expiry
At expiration for any contract in the money by at least $1.00

explanation: American options may be exercised early; OCC also auto-exercises many ITM contracts at expiration. Ops must process assignments whenever they occur.

distractorExplanations.b: That reverses the styles: American options allow early exercise, while European options are exercisable only at expiration.
distractorExplanations.c: OCC assigns exercise notices to clearing members on the exercise date itself; assignment is not deferred to expiration.
distractorExplanations.d: OCC exercise by exception applies at $0.01 in the money, and early exercise can trigger assignment before expiration anyway.

prompt: A customer's adult son emails a scanned power of attorney and asks operations to wire the entire account to a new bank the same day. What should operations do first?

options.text: Image the scan, change the mailing address to the son's residence, and release the wire
Review the scanned power of attorney under firm procedures before any wire
Open a new account titled to the son and journal the balance across the same day
Treat the son as the trusted contact and release the wire on his instruction

explanation: Operations may follow an agent's instructions only after it reviews the power of attorney, confirms the document is in force, and codes the agent on the account. An emailed scan is not authority to wire the balance the same day.

distractorExplanations.a: Imaging the scan and redirecting mail to the son's home follows the caller without establishing that the power of attorney is valid or that the agent has been authorized.
distractorExplanations.c: Journaling the assets into a new account for the son changes ownership; a power of attorney appoints an agent and does not make the son the owner.
distractorExplanations.d: A trusted contact under Rule 4512 may be asked about the customer's welfare but has no authority to order a wire or any other transaction.

prompt: Prime brokerage operations differ from retail back-office work partly because prime clients often need:

options.text: Mutual fund breakpoint tracking and 529 plan account servicing
Cash-account trading settled delivery versus payment at a custodian
Securities lending, margin financing, and consolidated reporting
Odd-lot dividend reinvestment and paper certificate safekeeping

explanation: Prime services support hedge funds and institutions with complex financing and reporting. Capital introduction is another common prime brokerage service.

distractorExplanations.a: Breakpoints and 529 plans are retail product servicing needs, not hedge fund financing and custody services.
distractorExplanations.b: DVP/RVP accounts settle at an outside custodian without financing; prime clients need leverage, borrows, and consolidated reporting.
distractorExplanations.d: DRIP and certificate safekeeping are retail services; prime brokerage centers on financing, securities lending, and reporting.

prompt: When a customer claims missing dividend payment, operations should first:

options.text: Verify ex-date trades and file a claim with the issuer's transfer agent
Verify declaration-date holdings and credit the dividend whenever the customer held the shares
Issue a goodwill credit for the dividend and research the break afterward
Verify record date holdings, payment date entries, and entitlements on the account

explanation: Dividend inquiries require reconciliation of positions on record date and cash postings.

distractorExplanations.a: Claims go to the counterparty or through DTC after research; the first step is reconciling the account's record date entitlement.
distractorExplanations.b: Entitlement depends on record date holdings, not on what the customer held on the declaration date.
distractorExplanations.c: Crediting before research risks a duplicate payment; ops must first confirm entitlement and posting.

prompt: Processing an IPO allocation involves operations ensuring:

options.text: Shares credit on settlement date with correct restricted status and cost basis
Shares credit on trade date at the first-day closing price as cost basis
Shares credit to restricted persons under Rule 5130 like other customers
Shares credit after the research quiet period ends for each allocated customer account

explanation: Allocations must reflect offering price, restrictions, and settlement through standard channels. This applies to each allocated customer account.

distractorExplanations.b: IPO cost basis is the public offering price, and shares post on settlement date, not at the first-day close on trade date.
distractorExplanations.c: Rule 5130 bars allocating new issues to restricted persons such as broker-dealer personnel; ops must exclude them.
distractorExplanations.d: The research quiet period limits analyst reports; it does not delay settlement of allocated IPO shares.

prompt: A global trade support desk covering multiple regions must coordinate:

options.text: U.S. settlement cycles applied to every market, with local holidays noted
Local market settlement cycles, holiday calendars, and currency cut-off times
Holiday calendars of the trade's home market, with FX settled on the trade date
Currency cut-off times in New York, since all FX settles through CHIPS

explanation: Cross-border ops aligns settlement dates and FX funding across jurisdictions. These matter most for cross-border trades.

distractorExplanations.a: Many foreign markets settle T+2 or on other cycles; applying the U.S. T+1 cycle everywhere causes cross-border fails.
distractorExplanations.c: Settlement needs both markets' calendars and FX funding within currency cut-offs (spot FX is T+2), not same-day FX on one calendar.
distractorExplanations.d: FX settles in each currency's home payment system (CLS, local RTGS), so desks track local cut-offs, not just New York CHIPS.

prompt: FINRA Rule 4511 requires firms to preserve books and records in:

options.text: Paper or electronic form, kept for three years when no other period is specified
Electronic form only, with paper records converted within one year
Any format the firm chooses, provided it keeps records for two years
A 17a-4 compliant format kept for each required retention period

explanation: FINRA Rule 4511(c) requires books and records to be preserved in a format and media that comply with SEA Rule 17a-4, and Rule 4511(b) sets a six-year retention default where FINRA rules and Rule 17a-4 specify no other period.

distractorExplanations.a: Rule 4511(b) sets a six-year default for records with no specified period under FINRA rules or 17a-4, not three years.
distractorExplanations.b: Rule 4511 and 17a-4 permit paper or compliant electronic records; there is no mandatory one-year paper conversion.
distractorExplanations.c: Records must be kept in a 17a-4-compliant format under 4511(c), and the default retention under 4511(b) is six years, not two.

prompt: FINRA Rule 4370 requires broker-dealers to establish:

options.text: Business continuity and contingency plans for critical operations
Written supervisory procedures for each office of supervisory jurisdiction
Annual CEO certification of compliance and supervisory processes
Customer account information records including a trusted contact

explanation: Rule 4370 mandates BCP addressing data backup, alternate sites, and critical function recovery.

distractorExplanations.b: Written supervisory procedures are required by Rule 3110; Rule 4370 is the business continuity plan rule.
distractorExplanations.c: The annual CEO certification is Rule 3130; Rule 4370 covers business continuity plans and emergency contacts.
distractorExplanations.d: Account information and trusted contact persons are FINRA Rule 4512, not the Rule 4370 business continuity rule.

prompt: The Bank Secrecy Act requires broker-dealers to:

options.text: File Currency Transaction Reports for cash deposits of $3,000 or more in a day
Implement AML programs including customer due diligence and suspicious activity monitoring
File Suspicious Activity Reports with FINRA for any suspicious transaction of $2,000 or more
Implement AML programs reviewed by an independent tester every five years

explanation: BSA/AML programs include CDD, SAR filings, and currency transaction reporting where applicable.

distractorExplanations.a: CTRs are filed for cash over $10,000 in a business day; $3,000 is the monetary instrument purchase recordkeeping threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: SARs are filed with FinCEN, not FINRA, and the broker-dealer threshold is $5,000; $2,000 is the money services business threshold.
distractorExplanations.d: FINRA Rule 3310 requires independent AML testing annually (every two years for certain firms), not every five years.

prompt: Customer Identification Program requirements under the Patriot Act mandate firms to:

options.text: Verify identity of customers using documentary methods, as non-documentary ones are barred
Verify identity of customers by obtaining each customer's Social Security card copy
Verify identity of customers opening accounts using documentary or non-documentary methods
Verify identity of account owners and file the CIP records with FinCEN each month

explanation: CIP collects name, address, DOB/formation date, and ID number with verification procedures.

distractorExplanations.a: The CIP rule expressly allows non-documentary methods such as credit bureau checks, alone or combined with documents.
distractorExplanations.b: CIP does not require an SSN card; it requires a taxpayer ID number and risk-based verification by documents or other means.
distractorExplanations.d: CIP records are kept by the firm for five years after the account closes; they are not filed with FinCEN.

prompt: A routing review finds that every marketable customer equity order goes to one affiliated wholesaler, and nobody compares those fills with other markets. What does FINRA Rule 5310 require?

options.text: Nothing further, because an exclusive route to an affiliated wholesaler is presumed to be best execution
Disclosure of the affiliate on the confirmation, after which the routing review may stop
A market comparison only after a customer complains that one fill was poor
Reasonable diligence to ascertain the best market, including other venues

explanation: FINRA Rule 5310 requires reasonable diligence to ascertain the best market so the customer's price is as favorable as possible under prevailing market conditions. An exclusive route to one affiliate, with no comparison of execution quality, skips that diligence. Disclosure and a later complaint do not replace the review.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats an exclusive affiliate route as automatically compliant. Rule 5310 requires a real look at the market, not a presumption that the affiliate is best.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops the duty at disclosure. Naming the affiliate on a confirmation does not replace the duty to ascertain the best market.
distractorExplanations.c: Makes best execution complaint-driven. Rule 5310 requires diligence on routing as orders are handled, not only after a customer objects to one fill.

prompt: Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board rules apply primarily to:

options.text: Broker-dealers and municipal advisors engaged in municipal securities activities
State and local issuers that sell municipal bonds to fund public projects
Broker-dealers trading corporate bonds and reporting those trades to TRACE
Banks and dealers in U.S. Treasury securities under the Government Securities Act

explanation: MSRB regulates municipal market professionals, not all businesses generally.

distractorExplanations.b: The MSRB cannot regulate municipal issuers directly; issuer disclosure is reached through dealer rules such as SEC Rule 15c2-12.
distractorExplanations.c: Corporate bond dealing and TRACE reporting are FINRA rules; MSRB rules govern municipal securities activities.
distractorExplanations.d: Treasury dealers are regulated under the Government Securities Act by Treasury, the SEC, and bank regulators, not the MSRB.

prompt: FINRA margin rules for pattern day traders require minimum equity of:

options.text: $2,000 in the margin account, the same minimum required to open any margin account
$25,000 in the margin account before day trading is permitted without restriction
$50,000 in the margin account, of which half may be met with a customer's cash account
$100,000 in the margin account, with day trading buying power limited to 2x equity

explanation: Under the current FINRA Rule 4210 pattern day trader provisions, the customer must hold at least $25,000 of equity in the margin account before day trading; below that level, day trading is restricted until the equity is restored.

distractorExplanations.a: $2,000 is the Rule 4210 minimum equity for a margin account; pattern day traders need $25,000.
distractorExplanations.c: PDT minimum equity is $25,000 and must be held in the margin account; cash-account balances do not count toward it.
distractorExplanations.d: The PDT minimum is $25,000, and day-trading buying power is up to 4x maintenance margin excess, not 2x equity.

prompt: FINRA Rule 4530 requires firms to report certain customer complaints when:

options.text: Complaints are made orally or in writing, once three are received from one customer
Complaints involve service delays and are not resolved within 30 days of receipt
Written complaints allege theft, misappropriation of funds or securities, or forgery
Complaints allege customer losses above $5,000, with the report due to FINRA within 90 days

explanation: FINRA Rule 4530 requires a prompt report when a written customer complaint alleges theft or misappropriation of funds or securities, or forgery. The trigger is that allegation. It is not a count of complaints from one customer, a service delay, or the size of a loss. Other written complaints are summarized on the quarterly report, but they are not this prompt filing.

distractorExplanations.a: 4530 reporting concerns written customer complaints; there is no three-complaints-per-customer trigger.
distractorExplanations.b: Service delays are not a 4530(a) trigger; 30 days is the deadline to report a specified event, not a complaint test.
distractorExplanations.d: 4530(a) events are reported within 30 days, and complaint reporting turns on the allegation type (theft, misappropriation, forgery), not a dollar amount.

prompt: Payment for order flow disclosure informs customers that:

options.text: The firm pays market makers a fee to execute orders at the NBBO midpoint
The customer's orders will be routed to the venue paying the highest rebate
The firm receives commissions from customers for each order it routes
The firm may receive compensation from market makers for routing orders

explanation: Rule 606/607 and Form CRS disclose PFOF and routing practices to retail customers.

distractorExplanations.a: PFOF flows from market makers to the broker, not from the broker to market makers.
distractorExplanations.b: PFOF does not override best execution; the firm must still route for the most favorable terms reasonably available.
distractorExplanations.c: Commissions are charged to customers; PFOF is compensation the firm receives from execution venues for routing.

prompt: SEC Rule 15c2-11 governs:

options.text: Publication of quotations for over-the-counter equity securities by broker-dealers
Continuing disclosure by municipal issuers that broker-dealers must review
Delivery of a preliminary prospectus to buyers 48 hours before confirmation
The net capital a broker-dealer must maintain relative to its aggregate indebtedness

explanation: Rule 15c2-11 requires a broker-dealer to have current issuer information before it publishes a quotation in an OTC equity. Municipal continuing disclosure, the IPO prospectus delivery rule, and the net-capital rule are different sections.

distractorExplanations.b: Municipal continuing disclosure obligations for underwriters are SEC Rule 15c2-12, not Rule 15c2-11.
distractorExplanations.c: The 48-hour preliminary prospectus delivery for IPOs is SEC Rule 15c2-8, not Rule 15c2-11.
distractorExplanations.d: Net capital requirements are SEC Rule 15c3-1; Rule 15c2-11 governs publishing quotations for OTC securities.

prompt: OFAC sanctions compliance requires broker-dealers to:

options.text: Screen customers against SDN lists at onboarding and on annual reviews
Screen customers and transactions against SDN and blocked lists
Report blocked transactions to FinCEN on a SAR within 30 calendar days
Screen wire beneficiaries against SDN lists but not the account holders

explanation: OFAC rules bar dealings with Specially Designated Nationals and other blocked persons, so broker-dealers screen customers and transactions continuously, block or reject matches, and report blocked property to OFAC within 10 business days.

distractorExplanations.a: Screening must cover transactions and list updates on an ongoing basis, not just onboarding plus an annual refresh.
distractorExplanations.c: Blocked or rejected transactions are reported to OFAC within 10 business days; SARs to FinCEN are a separate BSA filing.
distractorExplanations.d: OFAC compliance covers both customers and transactions; skipping account holders misses sanctioned account owners.

prompt: SEC Rule 17a-4 for electronic communications requires:

options.text: Retention of electronic communications for one year in any rewriteable electronic storage format
Backup on the firm email server, with deletion permitted after 90 days
Non-rewriteable, non-erasable format (or equivalent) for retained broker-dealer records
Retention of emails only, while instant messages and texts are excluded

explanation: WORM or audit-trail alternatives preserve books and records for examination.

distractorExplanations.a: Communications are kept at least three years under 17a-4(b)(4), in WORM or a compliant audit-trail system, not rewriteable storage.
distractorExplanations.b: Ordinary server backups with 90-day deletion fail both the three-year retention period and the 17a-4 format requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: 17a-4 covers business communications in any medium, including IMs, texts, and chats, as the SEC off-channel cases showed.

prompt: FINRA gift and gratuity rules under Rule 3220 limit:

options.text: Year-end awards the firm gives its own employees for strong performance
Gifts from customers to representatives, capped at $25 per occasion
Salary and commissions the broker-dealer pays registered employees
Gifts to other firms' employees relating to their employer's business

explanation: Rule 3220 limits gifts that a member or its associated persons give to employees or agents of another person when the gift relates to that employer's business; gifts above the annual per-person limit are prohibited. Ordinary business entertainment and the firm's own pay fall outside the rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Awards a firm gives its own employees are employment compensation; Rule 3220 targets gifts to people employed by others.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no $25 per-occasion cap; the Rule 3220 limit is a per-person annual amount on gifts relating to the recipient employer's business.
distractorExplanations.c: Regular compensation paid by the employing firm is ordinary employment pay and falls outside the Rule 3220 gift limit.

prompt: Proxy voting for shares held in street name is typically performed by:

options.text: The broker-dealer or designated agent sending proxy materials
The issuer's transfer agent mailing ballots to each beneficial owner
The Depository Trust Company voting as the nominee holder of record
The broker voting on every proposal at its discretion after 10 days

explanation: Beneficial owners receive voting instructions via broker; ops processes ballots and omnibus votes. The broker or its agent also records and submits customer voting instructions.

distractorExplanations.b: Transfer agents deal with registered holders; street-name owners get materials through their broker or its agent.
distractorExplanations.c: DTC issues an omnibus proxy to its participants; it does not vote beneficial owners' shares itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Under NYSE Rule 452 brokers may vote uninstructed shares on routine matters only, not on every proposal.

prompt: Personal trading policies for operations employees commonly require:

options.text: Duplicate confirms and statements sent to compliance, with no pre-clearance of the employee's personal trades
Pre-clearance of trades, restricted lists, and blackout periods around corporate actions
Disclosure of trades to the employer only for purchases of employer stock
Trading through the firm itself, with accounts at other firms left unreported

explanation: Operations staff can see nonpublic customer and firm information, so personal-trading policies use pre-clearance, restricted lists, and blackout periods. Duplicate statements alone, a limit to employer stock, or an unreported account at another firm do not cover that access.

distractorExplanations.a: Duplicate statements are common, but ops staff with MNPI access are typically also subject to pre-clearance and restricted lists.
distractorExplanations.c: Policies cover reportable personal securities trades generally, not just purchases of employer stock.
distractorExplanations.d: Rule 3210 requires prior written consent from the employer for accounts held at other firms; they cannot go unreported.

prompt: A customer's check was credited yesterday. The bank has now returned the check unpaid. Which entry reverses the deposit?

options.text: Debit cash a second time and credit commission revenue for the amount of the returned check
Debit the box on the stock record and credit transfer, as if the return were a certificate movement
Leave yesterday's cash credit standing and charge the returned check to another customer's free credit
Debit the customer payable and credit cash for the amount of the returned check

explanation: Crediting the check increased cash and the payable owed to that customer. When the bank returns the check unpaid, both sides come off: debit the customer payable and credit cash. The return is not commission revenue, not a movement of certificates, and not a loss to charge against a different customer's free credit.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is debiting cash again and calling the returned check commission revenue, which records income and raises cash the bank has taken back.
distractorExplanations.b: The error is reversing a returned check on the stock record. The check is cash, not a certificate moving from the box into transfer.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is leaving the false cash credit in place and taking the returned check from a different customer's free credit.

prompt: A cash account had no trades this quarter. It still holds shares and a cash balance. What does FINRA Rule 2231 require the firm to send?

options.text: A quarterly statement, because the account still has a position and a cash balance
No statement is due, because Rule 2231 waits for a trade to print during the quarter
A confirmation of the account's last trade, in place of the periodic statement
A yearly holdings letter, because a quiet account skips the quarterly statement

explanation: FINRA Rule 2231 requires an account statement at least quarterly when the account held a securities position or a money balance, even if no trade occurred in the quarter. A confirmation does not take the place of that statement, and a quiet account is not moved to a once-a-year letter.

distractorExplanations.b: The error is waiting for a trade to print before sending a statement. A position or a money balance during the quarter requires the statement.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is substituting a trade confirmation for the quarterly statement. A confirm reports one trade and does not replace the statement.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is pushing an account that still holds shares and cash to a yearly letter. The quarter still gets a statement.

prompt: Cost basis on Form 1099-B for covered securities generally reports:

options.text: Dividends and interest paid on covered securities during the year
Proceeds and basis for sales to assist customer tax reporting
Proceeds for sales, with basis left for the customer to compute
Year-end market value and basis of positions still held

explanation: Brokers report sales proceeds and basis on 1099-B per cost basis reporting rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Dividends and interest go on Forms 1099-DIV and 1099-INT; Form 1099-B reports proceeds and basis from sales.
distractorExplanations.c: For covered securities brokers must report adjusted basis; leaving basis to the customer describes noncovered lots.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 1099-B reports dispositions, not unrealized year-end holdings; unsold positions do not appear on it.

prompt: An incoming wire has no account number and was credited to suspense. At month-end the cashier wants to take that cash into firm revenue. What is the right treatment?

options.text: Take the wire into firm revenue when no customer has claimed it by month-end
Reclassify the wire as fully paid securities and move it into segregation
Keep the cash in suspense and research the owner before the firm uses it
Apply the wire to the largest margin debit so the firm's exposure falls

explanation: Suspense is holding cash that has not been identified. That cash is not firm revenue, it is not a securities position to segregate, and it is not a payment against another customer's debit. It stays in suspense while operations looks for the owner.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is taking unidentified customer cash into firm revenue at month-end because nobody has claimed it yet.
distractorExplanations.b: The error is turning a cash wire into fully paid securities and segregating it. The item in suspense is cash, not shares.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is applying an unidentified wire to the largest margin debit, which uses one customer's cash against another customer's loan.

prompt: Fully paid customer certificates are at a custodian bank that also holds a lien for a loan to the firm. Why does that fail as a control location?

options.text: A bank fails as a control location for customer certificates even when those certificates are free of lien
The lien is acceptable once the firm's latest reserve computation has been completed
The certificates should be entered on the cash blotter until the firm's loan is repaid
The lien lets the bank hold the certificates, so the firm does not control them

explanation: Certificates at a custodian bank support possession or control when the bank holds them free of lien and the firm can direct them for the customer. A lien securing the firm's own loan lets the bank keep those certificates. Completing the reserve computation does not remove the lien, and the certificates are not a cash-blotter entry.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is rejecting every bank location. A bank can be a control location when the certificates are free of lien.
distractorExplanations.b: The error is treating a finished reserve computation as a waiver of the bank's lien. The reserve cycle covers cash, not a lien on certificates.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is moving share certificates onto the cash blotter. The failed location is a securities control problem, not a cash entry.

prompt: End-of-day position reconciliation compares:

options.text: Internal ledgers to DTC/depository records and counterparty statements
Customer statements to trade confirmations sent during the period
Internal ledgers compared with the firm's cash accounts, leaving the security positions unchecked
The desk's trader positions set against each trader's profit-and-loss report for the day

explanation: Position breaks between books and depository must be researched and resolved promptly.

distractorExplanations.b: Statement-versus-confirm checks are a customer communications review, not a books-to-depository position reconciliation.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash reconciliation is a separate control; position reconciliation compares security positions to DTC and counterparties.
distractorExplanations.d: P&L-versus-position checks are a desk risk control; operations position recon compares books to depository records.

prompt: A customer requests a full transfer of a margin account that still carries a debit balance. What should the delivering firm include with the securities?

options.text: The long shares alone, leaving the debit at the delivering firm as its own receivable
The margin debit, so the account moves together instead of as a cash account
A free-credit balance created by writing the debit off before the transfer is sent
The equity in the account, with the debit left open on the delivering firm's books

explanation: A full transfer of a margin account moves the account as it stands: the securities and the debit go together. Leaving the debit behind, or writing it off so a cash account goes out, does not transfer the account the customer asked to move. Cash that arrives after the transfer is a later item, not a reason to drop the debit.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is sending the long shares and keeping the debit as the delivering firm's receivable, which splits the margin account.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is writing the debit off and creating a free credit so the transfer looks like a cash account.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is transferring equity value and leaving the debit open at the delivering firm instead of moving the debit with the securities.

prompt: Settled receipts of certificates are on the receipts-and-deliveries blotter, and the stock record is updated for where those certificates now sit. Which statement is right?

options.text: The receipts blotter should be erased once the stock record shows the new location.
The stock record should list each receipt as a permanent trade, replacing the blotter.
The receipts blotter records the movement, and the stock record shows the location.
Both records are wrong unless the receipt is removed from the blotter on the day the certificates reach the vault.

explanation: The receipts-and-deliveries blotter is an original-entry record of certificates coming in and going out. The stock record is the position book and shows the location after that movement. Updating the location does not authorize erasing the blotter, and the stock record does not become a second blotter of every receipt.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is treating the blotter as a temporary note that can be erased once the stock record is updated. The blotter remains the record of the movement.
distractorExplanations.b: The error is making the stock record do the blotter's job. The stock record shows where the position sits, not a permanent list of each receipt.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is requiring the blotter entry to come off when the certificates arrive. Arrival changes the stock-record location; it does not delete the receipt.

prompt: During a periodic securities count, the team copies the prior cycle's box totals onto the count sheet and does not open the vault. Why does that fail as a box count?

options.text: It is acceptable, because the stock record already states what the vault holds.
A supervisor's signature on the copied totals is enough to complete the count.
It is a valid count of positions at the depository, so operations can skip opening the vault and still sign the count as complete.
A box count must physically count the vault and then compare the result to the stock record.

explanation: A periodic box count under Rule 17a-13 is a physical examination of securities in the firm's possession, compared with the stock record. Copying the prior totals, even with a signature, does not count the vault. The box count is also not the procedure that proves positions at a depository.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is treating the stock record as a substitute for looking in the vault. The count exists so the record can be tested against the certificates.
distractorExplanations.b: The error is treating a signature on copied numbers as the count. Someone has to examine the securities, not just approve last cycle's totals.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is using a skipped vault exam to stand in for a depository reconciliation. Copying old totals counts neither the box nor the depository.

prompt: Before a sale settles, the customer names the purchased lot to use, and the firm can apply that instruction to the sale. Which shares are treated as sold?

options.text: The specific lot the customer identified for this sale
The earliest lot, because the FIFO default overrides the lot the customer named
The most recently purchased lot, because a written request is treated as LIFO
A blended average of every open lot, rather than the lot the customer named

explanation: When the customer identifies the lot in time for the firm to apply it to the sale, that lot is the one treated as sold. FIFO is the method used when no lot is identified. Naming a lot does not switch the sale to LIFO, and it does not produce an average of every open lot.

distractorExplanations.b: The error is letting the FIFO default override a lot the customer identified in time for the firm to apply it.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is reading a written lot request as LIFO. The shares sold are the lot the customer named, not the newest lot.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is averaging every open lot. A specific-lot instruction uses that lot, and average cost is a different method.

prompt: Customer shares that were in transfer are back from the transfer agent and belong in segregation. Which posting keeps the stock record reconcilable?

options.text: Increase segregation and leave the transfer location unchanged.
Decrease transfer and increase segregation by the same quantity.
Remove both locations and record a new fail to receive.
Credit the special reserve bank account for the returned shares and leave the transfer and segregation locations on the stock record exactly as they were.

explanation: Returning shares move from one stock-record location to another. Transfer comes down and segregation goes up by the same quantity, so location totals still equal the accounts. Raising segregation without releasing transfer double-counts the shares. A reserve-account credit does not record a certificate movement.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is adding the shares to segregation without taking them off transfer, which counts the same certificates in two locations.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is turning a completed return from the transfer agent into a fail to receive and dropping both real locations.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is booking certificates as a cash credit in the reserve account and leaving the stock-record locations stale.

prompt: A prime brokerage statement shows a rebate on the client's short position. What is that rebate?

options.text: A charge for each day the short sale has failed to settle at the clearing corporation
Interest the client owes on a margin debit that was opened by the short sale
A credit to the client related to cash collateral posted against the short
A safekeeping credit for fully paid long shares held in segregation for the client

explanation: A rebate on a short is a credit to the client on cash collateral posted against that short, as the prime agreement provides. It is not a charge for a fail to settle, it is not interest on a margin debit, and it is not a custody credit for segregated long shares.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is describing a settlement-fail charge. A rebate shown on the short is a credit tied to the collateral, not a fail fee.
distractorExplanations.b: The error is calling the rebate margin interest the client owes. A rebate is a credit on short collateral, not a debit-balance charge.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is treating the rebate as a safekeeping credit for segregated long shares. The line is about the short and its collateral.

prompt: Yesterday's purchase-and-sale blotter is stored at a vendor. An examiner asks the firm for that blotter. What is the firm's duty?

options.text: Send the examiner to the vendor and wait until the vendor decides to respond
Produce the blotter when the request names one customer, and withhold it otherwise
Treat the vendor contract as the end of the firm's duty to produce the blotter
Produce the blotter promptly; storage at a vendor does not move that duty

explanation: The firm has to produce a required blotter promptly when an examiner asks. A vendor may store the file, but the duty stays with the firm. Sending the examiner to the vendor, limiting production to a named customer, or treating the contract as the end of the duty leaves the request unanswered.

distractorExplanations.a: The error is handing the request to the vendor and waiting. The examiner asked the firm, and the firm has to produce the blotter.
distractorExplanations.b: The error is withholding the blotter unless one customer is named. The blotter is a firm record the examiner can ask for as a book.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is treating the storage contract as a transfer of the duty. The firm remains responsible for producing its blotter.

prompt: A carrying firm owes customers idle cash and also holds their fully paid shares. Which protection matches each asset?

options.text: Idle cash goes through the reserve computation; fully paid shares need possession or control.
One deposit to the reserve bank account covers both the idle cash and the shares.
Fully paid shares are covered by the reserve deposit, and idle cash is covered by segregation.
Idle cash needs no reserve because it is a firm asset, and fully paid shares may be delivered against the firm's own trades.

explanation: Idle cash owed to customers is a credit in the customer reserve computation and is protected by the special reserve bank account. Fully paid shares are protected by possession or control, not by that cash deposit. Reversing the two, or treating the cash as a firm asset the firm may deliver against, leaves customer property unprotected.

distractorExplanations.b: The error is using one reserve deposit to protect both cash and shares. The deposit covers customer cash credits; shares are a possession-or-control item.
distractorExplanations.c: The error is swapping the two protections. Segregation and other control locations cover the shares; the reserve deposit covers the cash.
distractorExplanations.d: The error is treating idle customer cash as firm money and treating fully paid shares as available for the firm's own deliveries.

prompt: When processing a forward stock split, operations adjusts:

options.text: Share quantity and total cost basis by the split ratio, while leaving price unchanged
Share quantity and price history while preserving total market value per account
Per-share cost basis upward by the split ratio for each affected lot
Price history, with cash in lieu paid for each whole share received

explanation: Splits multiply shares and divide price; total value unchanged absent fractional handling.

distractorExplanations.a: Total cost basis stays the same in a split; only per-share basis and price are divided by the split ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: In a forward split per-share basis is divided by the ratio, not increased; total basis stays the same.
distractorExplanations.d: Cash in lieu is paid for fractional shares; whole split shares are credited to the account as shares.

prompt: The dividend clerk calculates a cash dividend, approves the payment file, and releases the checks. What should the firm change?

options.text: Leave all three steps with that clerk and have a supervisor initial the monthly dividend report.
Let the clerk release the checks first and approve the same file the following week.
Waive approval when the dividend rate comes from the depository announcement.
Have a different person approve the file and another person release the checks.

explanation: Segregation of duties splits calculation, approval, and release of a cash dividend so the person who computes the payment cannot also approve the file and send the checks. One clerk in all three roles can overpay an account and sign off on the result. A monthly initial, a later self-approval, or a waiver because the depository announced the rate leaves those incompatible steps together.

distractorExplanations.a: A monthly initial after the checks go out does not separate the duties. Reviewing a report later is not a different approver and a different releaser.
distractorExplanations.b: Reordering the same clerk's work across a week is still one person. Segregation assigns approval and release to other people.
distractorExplanations.c: A depository announcement supports the rate. It does not authorize the clerk who calculated the file to approve and release it.

prompt: An outgoing wire over the firm's cashiering limit is queued for release. What does dual control require?

options.text: A second authorized person approves the release.
The person who entered the wire releases it after reading the amount back from the screen.
A chat message from the registered representative is treated as the second approval.
The overnight process releases every queued wire once the cutoff clock passes.

explanation: Dual control on cashiering means a second authorized person, who did not enter the wire, approves it before cash leaves the firm. The enterer confirming the figure, a chat from the representative, or an overnight job that releases the queue without that second approval leaves a single path from entry to payment.

distractorExplanations.b: The person who entered the wire is not a second controller. Rereading the screen is a self-check, and dual control requires someone else to approve the release.
distractorExplanations.c: A representative's chat is not cashiering dual control. The second approval comes from an authorized operations person, not from a message about urgency.
distractorExplanations.d: An automatic release at cutoff removes the second person. Dual control is an approval by another authorized person, not a clock.

prompt: A counterparty issues a buy-in notice on an undelivered municipal fail. Which action is the escalation?

options.text: Store the notice with the weekly settlement bundle and revisit it if the fail is still open then.
Give the notice and the open fail to the desk that must deliver the bonds or answer the notice.
Take the fail off the open report because a buy-in notice has arrived.
Ask the counterparty to cancel the notice so the firm can keep the bonds.

explanation: A buy-in notice on an undelivered fail is escalated at once to the desk that can deliver the bonds or answer the notice. Filing it in a weekly bundle, dropping the fail because the notice arrived, or asking that the notice be cancelled so the firm can keep the bonds leaves the buy-in unaddressed and puts the firm's preference ahead of delivery.

distractorExplanations.a: A weekly bundle is a delay. Escalation means the desk that owns the fail sees the notice while there is still a chance to deliver or respond.
distractorExplanations.c: Receiving a notice does not close the fail. Removing it from the open report hides the item the desk needs to see.
distractorExplanations.d: Asking the counterparty to cancel the notice so the firm can keep the bonds favors the firm. The desk delivers or answers the buy-in.

prompt: A continuity test shows the alternate operations site cannot retrieve the overnight settlement file. What should the firm do with that result?

options.text: Treat the test as successful because the primary site processed the same file without trouble.
Skip the next test so settlement staff are not pulled off the desk for another exercise.
Log the failed retrieval, fix the connection, and retest before relying on that site.
Remove the failed test from the review file so the record of the test shows no gap.

explanation: A continuity test that cannot retrieve the settlement file is an open gap at the alternate site. Operations logs that result, gets the connection fixed, and runs the test again before treating the site as ready. A working primary site does not pass the alternate-site test, skipping the next test leaves the gap in place, and deleting the failed result hides it from the review.

distractorExplanations.a: The primary site working does not test the alternate site. The failed retrieval is the result that has to be fixed and run again.
distractorExplanations.b: Skipping the next test avoids the inconvenience and leaves the alternate site unable to reach the file. A failed test is repaired and retested.
distractorExplanations.d: Deleting the failed result makes the review look clean. The gap remains until the connection is fixed and the retrieval is tested again.

prompt: Liquidity risk in brokerage clearing operations arises when:

options.text: The firm's proprietary inventory falls in value during a market decline
A customer fails to meet a margin call and the debit becomes unsecured
A system outage delays trade processing during the overnight settlement batch run
The firm cannot meet cash or securities settlement obligations on due dates

explanation: Clearing liquidity risk is failure to fund settlements—not customer investment performance.

distractorExplanations.a: Price declines in inventory are market risk; liquidity risk is about meeting settlement and funding obligations when due.
distractorExplanations.b: An unsecured margin debit is customer credit risk, not the firm's ability to fund its settlements.
distractorExplanations.c: System outages are operational risk, even though they may later contribute to funding problems.

prompt: A counterparty sends a don't-know on a sale that is still open on the firm's blotter. What should operations do first?

options.text: Keep the trade open as a break and research the mismatch with the desk before canceling it.
Cancel the blotter row the same day so the don't-know drops off the open-item report.
Reverse the customer's sale as soon as the don't-know arrives, before anyone reads the order ticket.
Move the trade into the error account and close the don't-know without identifying the mismatch.

explanation: A don't-know means the counterparty does not recognize a trade the blotter still shows. Operations leaves the trade open, researches the mismatch with the desk that booked it, and only then cancels or corrects. Canceling to clear the report, reversing the customer's sale before the ticket is read, or parking the trade in the error account removes the break before anyone knows which record is wrong.

distractorExplanations.b: Canceling the blotter row to clear the report hides the don't-know. The trade stays open until research shows whether the firm or the counterparty is wrong.
distractorExplanations.c: A don't-know does not by itself reverse the customer's sale. Operations reads the order ticket and the counterparty's claim before canceling the customer side.
distractorExplanations.d: The error account is for a known firm error, not a drawer for an unidentified don't-know. The break has to be explained before any account is changed.

prompt: Screening a new account produces a sanctions-list match, and a wire on that account is queued for release. What should operations do?

options.text: Release the wire because the representative already signed the new-account approval.
Hold the wire and escalate the list match before any funds leave the firm.
Ask the customer for a same-day note denying the match, then release the wire.
Change the spelling of the name so the screening list no longer returns a match.

explanation: A sanctions-list match stops the movement of funds. Operations holds the queued wire and escalates the match through the firm's screening process before cash leaves. The representative's account approval, a note from the customer, or a changed spelling does not clear a list hit.

distractorExplanations.a: New-account approval does not clear a sanctions-list match. The wire stays on hold until that hit is escalated and resolved.
distractorExplanations.c: A same-day denial from the customer is not a clearance. Releasing the wire on that note moves funds before the list match is resolved.
distractorExplanations.d: Changing the spelling to dodge the list conceals the hit. The name stays as it is, and the match is escalated rather than edited away.

prompt: A trade-error balance is still in the error account, and the trader asks to leave it there until a later gain can offset it. What should operations do?

options.text: Leave the balance in the error account so a later gain can offset it without supervisory review.
Move the balance into a customer account that can absorb it, so the error account looks clear.
Escalate the open balance for supervisory review and a supported correction.
Relabel the balance as a customer free credit so it no longer shows as a firm error.

explanation: An error-account balance is temporary. When it is still open and the desk wants to wait for an offsetting gain, operations escalates it for supervisory review and a correction that names the error. Leaving it to net against a future gain, moving it into a customer account, or relabeling it as a free credit hides a firm loss or assigns that loss to a customer.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for a later gain to offset the error leaves a firm loss unreviewed. An open error balance is escalated, not carried until it nets out.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving a firm error into a customer account assigns the firm's loss to that customer. The balance needs a supported correction, not a new home.
distractorExplanations.d: A free credit is customer cash. Relabeling a trade error as a free credit misstates both the error account and the customer's money.

prompt: The street side of a block is already matched, but the adviser has not affirmed which customer accounts receive the shares. What should operations do?

options.text: Settle the shares into the firm's inventory and move them to customers after the month closes.
Apply the previous day's account breakdown so the allocation can be released now.
Treat the missing affirmation as a don't-know and cancel the matched street trade.
Hold the customer allocation until the adviser affirms the account breakdown.

explanation: Once the street side is matched, the customer allocation still waits for the adviser's affirmation of which accounts receive the shares. Operations holds that allocation until the breakdown is affirmed. Parking the shares in firm inventory, reusing an older breakdown, or canceling a matched street trade treats a missing affirmation as a different problem.

distractorExplanations.a: Settling the block into firm inventory uses the firm's account as a holding pen. The shares wait for the affirmed allocation rather than moving onto the firm's books.
distractorExplanations.b: The previous day's breakdown belongs to a different trade. Using it releases shares to accounts the adviser has not affirmed for this block.
distractorExplanations.c: A missing customer affirmation is not a don't-know on a street trade that is already matched. The allocation waits; the street side is not canceled for that reason.

prompt: Cybersecurity incident response in operations should include:

options.text: Isolating affected systems, preserving logs, and notifying security leadership
Restoring affected systems from backup first, then reviewing logs afterward
Notifying all affected customers before isolating the compromised systems
Isolate the affected systems, then wait for FINRA approval before the firm starts sending wires again

explanation: Incident response contains damage and supports forensic review and regulatory reporting. Each step follows the firm's incident response playbook.

distractorExplanations.b: Restoring before preserving evidence can overwrite forensic data; containment and log preservation come first.
distractorExplanations.c: Containment comes first; customer notice follows Reg S-P and state breach laws once the scope is known.
distractorExplanations.d: FINRA does not approve resumption of operations; the firm decides under its incident response and BCP plans.

prompt: The stock-loan recall report and the firm's box position disagree by several hundred shares. What does the reconciliation control require?

options.text: Adjust the box position to the recall report so the two totals agree before the close.
Record the break, name an owner who did not book the loan, and research the shares before any change.
Net the share difference against a recall break in another security from an earlier month.
Drop the difference because the stock-loan system, rather than the customer book, produced the report.

explanation: When the recall report and the box disagree, the difference is a reconciliation break. The control records it, assigns an owner who did not book the loan, and researches the shares before any position is changed. Forcing the box to the report, netting another security, or dropping the item because stock loan produced the report makes the break vanish without identifying the shares.

distractorExplanations.a: Changing the box to match the report forces a balance. The break stays open until research shows which record is wrong and why.
distractorExplanations.c: A break in another security, including one from an earlier month, is a separate item. Netting them explains neither difference.
distractorExplanations.d: Which system produced the report is not a reason to ignore a share difference. A stock-loan break is reconciled like any other position break.

prompt: After the street trade prints, operations finds the shares were allocated to the wrong customer account. What does that error require?

options.text: No correction, if the two accounts happen to share the same mailing address on file.
A books-and-records note only, with the shares left in the account that received them.
A prompt correction of the allocation and a review of harm to the customer who was left out.
A bust of the street execution with the counterparty, because the allocation account named on the confirm was wrong.

explanation: Allocating a printed trade to the wrong account puts the shares in the wrong place. Operations corrects the allocation and reviews whether the customer who should have received the trade was harmed. A shared mailing address does not make the accounts interchangeable, a note that leaves the shares where they are does not fix the error, and a bad allocation does not by itself void a valid street execution.

distractorExplanations.a: A shared mailing address does not make two accounts the same recipient. The shares still have to move to the account that was supposed to receive the trade.
distractorExplanations.b: A note that leaves the shares in the wrong account records the mistake and does not correct it. The allocation has to be moved.
distractorExplanations.d: A wrong allocation account does not by itself void the street execution. The usual correction moves the position to the right customer, rather than busting a valid street trade.

prompt: A transfers supervisor can grant production entitlements and can also approve the account transfers those rights allow. What should change?

options.text: Add full customer tax identifiers to the same screen so the supervisor can work faster.
Issue one group login for the transfer team and let the supervisor hold the password.
Review the supervisor's access only after an incident has already been declared.
Remove entitlement administration from the person who approves the transfers.

explanation: Information entitlement keeps administration of access apart from the business action that access permits. A transfers supervisor who can both grant production rights and approve transfers can give anyone, including themselves, the ability to approve movements. The administration right comes off that person. More customer data on the screen, a group password, or a review that waits for an incident leaves the combination in place.

distractorExplanations.a: Adding tax identifiers increases the data exposed to a person who already administers access. The fix removes the combined duties rather than adding data.
distractorExplanations.b: A group login held by the supervisor hides who approved a transfer and who granted the right. Entitlements stay individual, and administration stays separate.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for an incident leaves the incompatible rights in place. Entitlement design separates administration from transfer approval before something goes wrong.

prompt: Operations is asked to sign off a sales-system release that changes how order tickets route to the branch. What is that sign-off confirming?

options.text: Tested routing matches the approved business requirement.
The vendor's implementation team has already installed the release in the production region.
Branch staff will be told to work around any ticket that routes to the wrong desk.
The previous release was stable, so this routing change needs no separate check.

explanation: Sign-off on a sales-system release confirms that testing shows the change meets the approved business requirement, here the rule for which desk receives an order ticket. Installation by the vendor, a workaround for misrouted tickets, or comfort with the previous release does not establish that this routing change does what the firm approved.

distractorExplanations.b: Installation means the software is present. It does not confirm that tickets route the way the approved requirement describes.
distractorExplanations.c: A workaround accepts misrouting. Validation is supposed to show the requirement is met before staff are told to cope with bad tickets.
distractorExplanations.d: Stability of the previous release says nothing about this routing change. Each approved requirement is validated on its own test.

prompt: A coworker wants to email the firm's SAR to the customer's bank so the bank can freeze the account. What should the associate do?

options.text: Send the SAR, because the customer's bank is another financial institution and can receive a copy.
Refuse the request to email the customer's bank a copy of the SAR.
Read the SAR at the next branch meeting so representatives will stop taking orders from that customer.
Delete the SAR from the firm's files so there is nothing left that could be emailed.

explanation: SAR confidentiality does not allow a courtesy copy to the customer's bank. That send can reach the subject of the report. The associate refuses the email. Treating another firm as automatically entitled to the SAR, briefing the branch, or deleting the filing are further disclosures or destruction of a report the firm must keep confidential.

distractorExplanations.a: The customer's bank is not automatically entitled to a copy of the SAR. Emailing it there discloses the filing and can tip off the subject.
distractorExplanations.c: Reading the SAR at a branch meeting spreads the filing to people who do not need it and can carry it to the customer. Confidentiality limits who learns that a report was filed.
distractorExplanations.d: Deleting the file does not answer the sharing request and destroys the record of the filing. The report stays in place, and the copy to the bank is refused.
